readings.title: Finding a leak in a shared building
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
An apartment building used more water than usual. Residents blamed longer showers, but the increase continued after several families travelled away. The main obstacle was a rise that household habits did not explain. The building had no routine comparison of night-time readings when taps were rarely used. At first, the people involved did not agree on which part of the proposal deserved the most attention.

To investigate, the team used meter readings at quiet hours. A qualified maintenance worker compared daily records and inspected accessible pipes. The organizers kept the first stage small enough to change without wasting substantial time or resources.

The evidence indicated a hidden toilet valve ran continuously. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced a prompt repair and a monthly meter log. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. The records were useful because they described ordinary use rather than an ideal situation imagined at a meeting.

The case suggests a broader point: simple records can reveal waste that people cannot see. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. The group published its reasons so that people who preferred a different result could still understand the choice. For those taking part in finding a leak in a shared building, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records.

readings.title: Watering a school garden wisely
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A school garden looked dry at midday. Pupils watered it every afternoon, yet some plants weakened and the soil stayed wet below the surface. The main obstacle was watering decisions based only on appearance. The top layer dried quickly while roots remained in damp soil. The question mattered to people with different schedules and levels of experience, so one account could not represent everyone.

To investigate, the team used soil checks at consistent depths. Teachers asked pupils to compare conditions before and after watering without damaging the plants. A simple record of what happened each day gave the team a starting point for comparison.

The evidence indicated some beds received more water than needed. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced a schedule guided by soil condition and weather. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. Some participants welcomed the change immediately, while others noticed practical details that needed further work.

The case suggests a broader point: careful observation improves conservation. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. The result was a revised plan, not a claim that every difficulty had disappeared. For those taking part in watering a school garden wisely, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: Explaining a public water notice
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A town issued a notice about temporary water restrictions. Residents understood that they should save water but could not tell which activities were covered. The main obstacle was rules expressed in broad terms. The notice used technical categories instead of familiar examples from daily life. The initial idea sounded reasonable, yet the details of the place made it harder to carry out than expected.

To investigate, the team used a reading exercise with local households. Staff asked people to identify whether common activities were allowed under the notice. Instead of relying on a single opinion, the team invited several users to describe what they actually did.

The evidence indicated specific examples reduced uncertainty. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced a plain-language list with dates and contact details. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. This allowed the organizers to separate a temporary inconvenience from a pattern that required attention.

The case suggests a broader point: clear rules make shared conservation possible. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. They also decided when to check the arrangement again, because conditions could change over time. For those taking part in explaining a public water notice, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: Refilling bottles at a station
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A railway station installed a bottle-refill tap. Few passengers used it, although a nearby shop sold many bottled drinks. The main obstacle was a refill point hidden beyond ticket gates. Travellers could not see the tap from the main waiting area or find it on station maps. The people affected were invited to comment before a permanent arrangement was chosen.

To investigate, the team used a route observation with first-time visitors. The station team watched where people looked for water and recorded the most common paths. The first trial produced both useful results and questions the team could not yet answer.

The evidence indicated visibility mattered more than demand. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced direction signs and a map update near the entrance. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. Rather than hide those limits, the public note explained how the next version had been selected.

The case suggests a broader point: a sustainable service must be easy to find. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. That explanation made later changes easier to discuss with residents and staff. For those taking part in refilling bottles at a station, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

translation.stem:
Translate the following passage into Chinese:
A useful plan for urban water use and conservation must take account of the people who will use it. An idea may look complete on paper and still create difficulties during an ordinary week. Organizers therefore tried the urban water awareness programme on a small scale and invited comments from users with different schedules. They recorded benefits as well as the time and resources needed to provide them. Some findings supported the original aim, while others suggested that the method should change. The group published both kinds of result instead of presenting the trial as a simple success or failure. This allowed residents to discuss the next step with a clearer understanding of its possible effects.

translation.referenceAnswer: 关于城市水资源与节水的有用方案必须考虑实际使用它的人。一个想法在纸上看似完整，平常使用时却仍可能出现困难。因此，组织者小规模试行该服务，并邀请时间安排不同的使用者提出意见。他们既记录益处，也记录提供这些益处所需的时间和资源。有些发现支持最初目标，另一些则表明方法应当调整。团队同时公布两类结果，而没有把试行简单说成成功或失败。这让居民能更清楚地了解可能的影响，再讨论下一步。

writing.stem: Write at least 100 words in English to the local water team about a community activity related to urban water use and conservation. Explain how different people can participate, what should be recorded, and how the results should be shared.
writing.explanation: 范文供考生自评，注意任务要点、组织结构及语言准确性。
writing.sampleAnswer:
Dear Committee Members,
I would like to propose a small improvement to the urban water awareness programme. People have noticed a rise that household habits did not explain, and a short trial could help us understand how often this problem occurs. We should ask regular users and people who have not used the service before to describe their experiences. Their comments may reveal details that a plan made in an office would miss.
For one month, staff could keep a simple record of participation, time spent and any difficulties reported. We should also explain the purpose of the trial in clear language so that residents know how to contribute. After the month, please publish a brief summary of both benefits and limits. The final decision should be based on what people actually experienced, with a date for checking the arrangement again.
Yours sincerely,
A resident
